items.name: Leonida
items.description: Leonida Is A Native PC Recompilation Of The Xbox Version Of Grand Theft Auto 6
items.readme:
Leonida

Grand Theft Auto VI (Xbox Series) running natively on Windows, built on your PC from your own copy.

Status | How to build | How it works | Want to help? | Credits | License | Discord

Leonida is a static recompilation project. The Xbox Series CPU is x86-64 like a PC, so the game's code is loaded and run natively, and the console's system software is reimplemented. The console's precompiled RDNA2 GPU programs are translated to SPIR-V for Vulkan. The game's models, textures and audio are read from your package. All of this happens **on your PC, from your own copy of the game**. > [!IMPORTANT] > This repository **does not contain the game, keys or an executable**, and it does not explain how to get them. You > need your own copy, with its files already readable on disk. Nothing here decrypts or works around any protection. > Everything the build creates (the generated shaders, extracted assets, the runtime folder and your saves) comes > from your game and stays on your PC. Never share those files. Discord: https://discord.gg/rexed
## Project status **Early. The game does not boot yet.** Everything that can be done without the game's executable is in place, so work on booting can start as soon as one is available to a developer. | What | Status | |---|---| | Finding and checking your copy (Xbox Series 1.0.2.1) | ✅ Works | | Shaders: carve, unpack native RDNA2 code, disassemble | ✅ All 26,503 | | Shaders: RDNA2 → SPIR-V translation | ✅ **All 26,503**: 2,236 VS, 12,101 PS, 2,689 CS, 9,282 mesh, 195 geometry. All pass `spirv-val`, with a per-shader metadata index for pipeline creation. ⚠️ 21,545 are wave64: exact on 64-wide subgroups (AMD), and cross-half wave ops are approximate on 32-wide (NVIDIA) | | Shader translator checked on a real GPU | ⚠️ Vertex fetch, texture sampling, exports, ALU ops, partial-register ops, barycentrics, wave-uniform branches and compute (LDS, barriers, buffer stores) checked on one GPU | | Models (OBJ with real names, UVs, material references) | ✅ Exported. Not all layouts are decoded yet | | Texture dictionaries and world texture pools (DDS) | ✅ Exported. Some pool entries (BCPack) are skipped | | Audio banks (AWC: Opus, XMA2) | ✅ Exported whole. Opus repackaged **losslessly** as Ogg Opus; PCM (codec 0/2) as WAV; XMA2 decoded with ffmpeg. `--wav` adds 16-bit PCM WAV ([notes](docs/audio.md)) | | Music/radio config | ? Measured. **1,589** audio-config records with exact durations and AWC stream ids; station grouping and content-id lists; no per-track start offsets ([notes](docs/audio_config.md)) | | PE loader and import shims | ⚠️ Skeleton. Untested against the real executable | | Xbox D3D12 → Vulkan | ⚠️ In progress. A Vulkan-backed device behind the Xbox-ABI proxy creates queues, command lists, fences, descriptor heaps, views and committed resources; barriers, clears, uploads and copies (BC included) run on Vulkan, checked on one GPU. No shader views, pipelines, draws or swapchain yet ([plan](docs/d3d12_vulkan.md)) | | Booting, story mode, anything playable | ❌ No | ## How to build The port isn't downloaded ready-made. It's built on your PC from your own copy. **The easy way:** 1. Install the prerequisites below. 2. Download this project **with its submodule**: `git clone --recursive https://github.com/ItsNotRexed/Leonida`. A "Download ZIP" from GitHub leaves out `third_party/rpf9-explorer`. The build fetches it if `git` is installed, and otherwise tells you what to do. 3. Double-click **`Build.bat`**. It finds your copy of the game by itself: it looks in Downloads, Desktop, Documents, Games, your home folder and the top of every drive, two folders deep. It recognises the version from a few file sizes, without reading anything large. If you have more than one copy it asks which one, and if it finds none it asks you to paste the folder. Before starting it checks that everything below is installed and that there is enough free space, and it lists anything missing in one go. The result goes to `Documents\Leonida`. A stopped build continues where it left off. Your game folder is the one that holds `MicrosoftGame.Config` and the `.rpf` archives, as plain files. **Prerequisites:** - **Your own copy** of the Xbox Series package, version 1.0.2.1. - **Windows 10/11 x64**, with about **350 GB** free for work files. They can go on another drive with `--work`. - [Python 3.11+](https://www.python.org/downloads/) (tick "Add python.exe to PATH"). - [.NET 8 SDK](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/8.0). - [Vulkan SDK](https://vulkan.lunarg.com/), for `spirv-as` / `spirv-val`. - [LLVM 21+](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/releases) with the **AMDGPU target** for `llvm-mc`. The official Windows build has no AMDGPU target. On Windows, `scripts\build_llvm_mc.ps1` builds a native `llvm-mc.exe` with it (no WSL; needs git and the Visual Studio C++ tools below) and sets `LLVM_MC`. Or install `llvm-21` in WSL and set `LLVM_MC` to the whole command, `LLVM_MC="wsl -d Ubuntu -e /usr/lib/llvm-21/bin/llvm-mc"` (see [docs/design.md](docs/design.md#disassembling-shaders)). On Linux, `llvm-mc` on PATH is enough. - Visual Studio 2022 with **Desktop development with C++**, for the runtime stage. - [ffmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/download.html) on PATH (optional: decodes the XMA2 streams, and required for `--wav`). **From a terminal**, with the same behaviour and more control: ```powershell python -I make_game.py --find # list the copies found on this PC python -I make_game.py --check # check your copy, build nothing python -I make_game.py --game "D:\path\to\your\package" --out "D:\Games\Leonida" --work "E:\leonida-work" python -I make_game.py --stages shaders,assets # only some stages python -I make_game.py --game "D:\path\to\your\package" --wav # also decode Opus to PCM WAV (large) ``` Stages run in order: `check`, `shaders`, `assets`, `runtime`, `pipelines` (creates every translated shader on your GPU driver and saves a pipeline cache, so the first boot doesn't compile them). The shader translation is the longest step: it runs on `--jobs` processes (half the CPU threads by default). `--wav` is off by default because 16-bit PCM WAV is several times larger than Ogg Opus. It decodes the repackaged Ogg Opus streams to `work\assets\audio\wav` after the audio bank step; existing WAV files are skipped when a build resumes. ### Vulkan diagnostics on Linux With CMake 3.24+, a C++20 compiler, and Vulkan development headers and loader installed: ```sh cmake -S runtime -B runtime/build/linux cmake --build runtime/build/linux --parallel ./runtime/build/linux/vk_pipeline_check /path/to/spirv ``` Pass the directory containing `index.json` and the translated SPIR-V files to `vk_pipeline_check`. ## How it works | Piece | What it does | Where | |---|---|---| | Version check | Every package file's name, size and SHA-256 for each supported version | `game/`, `make_game.py` | | Shader pipeline | Carves DXBC containers from `shaders.rpf` without its encrypted table of contents. Unpacks the `XBCH` → `FSSM` native RDNA2 program, disassembles it with LLVM (`gfx1013`) and translates it to SPIR-V | `tools/shader_carve.py`, `fssm_unpack.py`, `shader_disasm.py`, `rdna2spirv.py` | | Asset export | Finds validated resources inside RPF9 archives and the loose `.ttpf` texture pools | `tools/rpf9dump` (on rpf9-explorer's Core) | | Runtime | Maps the PE image, resolves imports to shims (GDK, XMem, `d3d12_xs`) | `runtime/` | | Research tools | PE/RTTI inspection, raw carving, texture tiling probes, GPU test harnesses | `tools/`, `runtime/test/` | The translator's runtime contract (user SGPRs, push constants, memory model, bindless images, vertex fetch, system values) and all the format notes are in [docs/design.md](docs/design.md); the format, asset, runtime and validation notes are indexed in [docs/README.md](docs/README.md). The Xbox D3D12 plan is in [docs/d3d12_vulkan.md](docs/d3d12_vulkan.md). Audio bank formats and the export tools are in [docs/audio.md](docs/audio.md); [docs/related_projects.md](docs/related_projects.md) records the prior art we may read and the licence limits on it. ## Want to help? The biggest open pieces: - **Compute, mesh and geometry shaders**: their per-stage system-value register layout. - **Xbox D3D12 → Vulkan**: the `d3d12_xs` command list and descriptor heap model. - **Model layouts** the decoder rejects today. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Never attach game files, extracted assets or generated shaders to issues or pull requests. ## Credits - [rpf9-explorer](https://github.com/breadbbbb/rpf9-explorer) by breadbbbb: the RPF9 model, texture-pool and AWC decoders used by `tools/rpf9dump` (git submodule). - [Mesa](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/mesa/mesa) (MIT): GFX10 resource-descriptor layout (`tools/gfx10_formats.json`), and the ACO/RADV rules used as reference for 16-bit results and shader system registers. - [LLVM](https://llvm.org/): AMDGPU disassembler. - Logo: ["Grand Theft Auto VI" icon by SlyDevil](https://www.steamgriddb.com/icon/122618) on SteamGridDB. - [SPIRV-Tools](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/SPIRV-Tools): assembly and validation. Grand Theft Auto and all related names are trademarks of their owners. This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by them. ## License GPLv3 (or any later version). See [LICENSE](LICENSE). Third-party code keeps its own license.

items.name: rust-anything
items.description: Rewrite your whole app in Rust, one piece at a time, checked against the original's recorded behavior at every step. CLIs, HTTP servers and libraries in TypeScript, Python, C, Go, Ruby and Java.
items.readme:
rust-anything

Rewrite your whole app in Rust. Keep it working the whole way.

CLIs, servers and libraries, piece by piece, checked against the original at every step.

up to 20x faster · 38,251 recorded cases replayed · 0 mismatches · one command

**Rewrite your whole app in Rust, one piece at a time.** rust-anything records what your TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, C, Go, Ruby or Java app does today, then checks every piece of the Rust rewrite against that recording before it moves on, until the app is pure Rust. CLIs, HTTP servers and libraries; your coding agent (or you) writes the Rust. It can only catch what the recording covers: see [What it can't catch](#what-it-cant-catch). Only need the slow part fast? Port just that, one hot path at a time: | Real workload, same results as the original | Original | With rust-anything | | --- | ---: | ---: | | x18n's sidebar search, 50,000 keys (TypeScript, Node) | 10 ms per query | **0.5 ms: 20x faster** | | The same search in the browser (wasm, one thread) | 10 ms | **0.95 ms: 11.5x** | | `slugify` over 20,000 strings (Python) | 98 ms | **17x faster** | | `Shellwords.shellescape` from Ruby's standard library, 50,000 values | 88 ms | **11.8x faster** | | `Slugify` over 50,000 strings (Go) | 49 ms | **4x faster** | | `slugify` over 50,000 strings (Java) | 43 ms | **3x faster** |

Measured on 4 cores; every number has a benchmark in [`demo/`](./demo) that first checks the results are identical. Calling Rust once per small function is usually *slower* than a JIT; rust-anything finds the loop worth moving, and moves it. > rust-anything is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by the Rust Project > or the Rust Foundation. "Rust" is a trademark of the Rust Foundation. ## Quick start Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Gemini CLI and let your agent install it: ```text Install rust-anything: run `cargo install rust-anything`, then `rust-anything setup`. Tell me when to restart you. ``` Or yourself: ```sh cargo install rust-anything # from crates.io rust-anything setup # registers it with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI ``` No Rust toolchain yet? Prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux and Windows are attached to each [GitHub release](https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything/releases), and for JavaScript projects `npm install -g rust-anything` installs the same binary. In Claude Code you can also install it as a plugin (the MCP server and the skill; the CLI above must be on your `PATH`): ```text /plugin install rust-anything --marketplace erkamyaman/rust-anything ``` `setup` adds the MCP server to each agent it finds and installs the workflow skill where the agent reads skills. It keeps your other settings, is safe to run again, and `--remove` undoes it. Then ask your agent, for example: - *"Rewrite this CLI in Rust with rust-anything, end to end, and prove it behaves the same."* - *"This search feels slow. Profile it with rust-anything and move the hot loop to Rust."* - *"Plan a migration of `src/parser/` to Rust with rust-anything; port the first unit and prove it."* - *"Bench the Rust port in `rust/text-rs` against the original and tell me whether to ship it."* ### Works with | Agent | `rust-anything setup` adds | | --- | --- | | Claude Code | MCP server in `~/.claude.json`, skill in `~/.claude/skills/` | | Codex | MCP server in `~/.codex/config.toml`, skill in `~/.codex/skills/` | | Cursor | MCP server in `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | | Gemini CLI | MCP server in `~/.gemini/settings.json` | | Any other MCP client | add `rust-anything mcp` as a stdio server by hand (see [Install](#install)) | Before changing a file that exists, `setup` saves a copy beside it (`.rust-anything.bak`). Or run the steps yourself:

```sh rust-anything profile . -- node bench.mjs # what is hot, and who calls it rust-anything bridge . src/fuzzy.ts --batch fuzzyScore:text # write src/port.rs (or let your agent), then: rust-anything record rust/fuzzy-rs && rust-anything build rust/fuzzy-rs rust-anything diff rust/fuzzy-rs # every recorded case must match rust-anything bench rust/fuzzy-rs # faster? the verdict says rust-anything gate rust/fuzzy-rs # done means this passes ``` rust-anything does not translate code: your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, ...) or you write the Rust. rust-anything supplies what an agent cannot guess reliably: where the time goes, what to port first and in which order, a bridge so the rest of the code calls the Rust with its API unchanged, the exact behavior the port must match, a safe way to ship it, and a gate that says when a port is done. ## Languages | Language | Unit | Bridge | Recorded and replayed by | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | TypeScript/JavaScript | folder or file | napi-rs or wasm-bindgen with a generated binary wire; classes and async included | Node, running the `.ts` sources | | Python | package or module | PyO3 (abi3), direct conversion, typed exceptions | Python, importing the original | | C | `.c` file | `extern "C"` functions with the original names and a header | the original compiled to a shared library, called through ctypes, one fork per case | | Go | package | typed cgo calls and a generated binary wire, in a package with the original API | a generated Go driver, built as its own module | | Ruby | file or folder of module functions | a magnus extension under the original modules | a generated Ruby driver | | Java | package of `public static` methods | typed JNI and a generated binary wire, in wrapper classes with the original methods | a generated reflection driver | | PHP (preview) | folder of functions and `public static` methods | coming next: PHP FFI over a C ABI | whole apps today: `app record`, `app replay` and the front door, for CLIs and servers (`php -S`) | | C# (preview) | folder of `public static` methods | coming next: P/Invoke over a C ABI | whole apps today: `app record`, `app replay` and the front door, for CLIs and ASP.NET servers (`dotnet .dll`) | Every language except C also gets batch classes (`--batch`): the items cross once and stay in Rust, and each call runs over all of them on all cores. The language is detected from the repository (`go.mod`, `pom.xml`, a `.csproj` or `.sln`, `pyproject.toml`, `Gemfile`, `composer.json`, `package.json`, else the most common source files); `--lang` overrides it. Types come from the source: TS types, Python hints, C, Go, Java and C# signatures, Ruby YARD tags, PHP types and phpdoc; untyped parameters used as numbers are inferred as numbers. PHP is in preview: `analyze` plans a PHP app (Composer packages and PSR-4 autoloading, risks such as loose comparison and integer overflow into floats, Composer packages mapped to crates), and a PHP CLI or server can be recorded, replayed and put behind a Rust front door. Porting its units into Rust through PHP's FFI is the next step ([issue #2](https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything/issues/2)). C# is in preview the same way: `analyze` reads `.csproj` projects and their NuGet packages (mapped to crates), resolves `using` directives to folders, and flags what C# does differently (`decimal`, `dynamic`, LINQ's deferred queries, `Task`, `lock`, reflection). A C# CLI or ASP.NET server can be recorded, replayed and put behind a Rust front door; porting units through P/Invoke comes next. ## How it works ``` profile ──> analyze ──> bridge ──> record ──> port.rs ──> diff ──> bench ──> shadow ──> gate where the what to the Rust what the you or every faster? both side done means time goes port first crate and original your agent recorded the by side in this passes wrapper does write it case verdict production ``` The original stays the source of truth: `record` runs it on edge cases (and your own inputs) and saves what it returns or throws; `diff` replays every case against the Rust; nothing ships until they all match and `gate` passes. Callers keep the original API throughout. A whole app goes through the same loop unit by unit, inside a frame that proves the whole program ([Port a whole app](#port-a-whole-app)): ``` analyze --whole-app ──> app record ──> app front-door ──> per unit: the loop above, then app wire ──> app lift shape, every what the app Rust owns the gate passes, so the unit answers in pure Rust, dependency, the does from the entry point; the Rust: replay 100%, fallback rate down proved by decisions to make outside original answers replay ``` ## The loop | Step | Command | What it does | | --- | --- | --- | | 0. Profile | `rust-anything profile -- node bench.mjs` | Runs a real workload under the language's profiler (node, cProfile, `go test` pprof, JFR, a Ruby tracer): hot functions by inclusive time, their callers, and which loops to batch; flags code that is already compiled (numba, Cython, JAX), where Rust gains little | | 1. Plan | `rust-anything analyze ` | Units, port order, risks with `file:line`, bridge per unit, dependency-to-crate fit, best first ports; `--whole-app` adds entry points and shape, every dependency (imported or declared) with its crate, pieces (units that import each other move together) and numbered decisions with a recommended answer | | 2. Bridge | `rust-anything bridge ` | Crate with the bindings (`lib.rs`, plus the wrapper the source language loads) and stubs to port (`port.rs`); `--batch fn:param` adds a class that keeps many `param` values in Rust | | 3. Record | `rust-anything record ` | Runs the original on generated edge cases (non-ASCII, emoji, `-0`, `NaN`, ints where floats are expected, ...) and on every semantic trap in every parameter (string length and case, signed division, overflow edges, float printing, map and sort order), and saves `cases.jsonl`; `--float-tolerance 1e-9` lets floats match within that share for numeric code | | 3. Build | `rust-anything build ` | Builds the Rust side: `.node`, wasm package, Python extension or shared library | | 3. Diff | `rust-anything diff ` | Replays the recorded cases against Rust, called the way the original's callers call it; lists mismatches | | 3. Bench | `rust-anything bench ` | Times the recorded cases on the original and on Rust, bridge included | | 4. Shadow | `rust-anything shadow ` | Drop-in that runs both, returns the original's result, reports mismatches; `RUST_ANYTHING_MODE=old\|shadow\|new` | | 5. Gate | `rust-anything gate ` | fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, tests, `unsafe` audit, nothing unported, a recorded failing case for every error path of the original, no `unwrap`/`expect`/`panic!` where the original returns an error (unless marked `// INFALLIBLE: `), build, API, behavior | | Agents | `rust-anything setup` | Registers the MCP server (`rust-anything mcp`, every step as a tool) and the workflow skill ([`skills/rust-anything/SKILL.md`](./skills/rust-anything/SKILL.md)) with your coding agents | ## Port a whole app The goal is a pure Rust app that behaves like the original, with the original kept as reference. Your agent writes the Rust; rust-anything orders the work, scaffolds it, and proves every step. The [whole-app skill](./skills/rust-anything/whole-app.md) walks the agent through it, starting with the decisions only you can make: - **Grilling**: the agent asks in rounds, each question with its recommended answer, until every decision the port depends on is settled, and writes each one as an ADR in `rust/DECISIONS.md`, with `rust/GLOSSARY.md` mapping the original's terms to Rust names. - **Research**: background agents read each dependency's primary sources and write `rust/research/.md`, with every semantic trap they found. - **Across sessions**: `rust/MAP.md` lists every unit with its state; a session claims one unit before it starts, and each checkpoint leaves a `rust/HANDOFF.md` for the next session. Units in one wave can be ported in parallel by subagents. - **Cutover**: the agent does what it can and writes `rust/cutover.sh`, an interactive script for the steps only you can do (deploys, DNS, secrets), with a way back at each step. Grilling, research and these practices are adapted from [Matt Pocock's skills](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills). Plan first: `rust-anything analyze . --whole-app` adds the app's shape (CLI, server or library) and entry points, every external dependency (imported or declared) with its Rust crate and fit, the port order as pieces (units that import each other move together), and numbered decisions with a recommended answer: keep units, blocked units, dependencies with no or a partial crate. Then prove the whole program from the outside. `record` and `diff` prove one unit; `app record` and `app replay` prove the app, for CLIs and servers in any of the six languages (the app is a black box): ```sh rust-anything app record . -- python3 cli.py # the command that runs the original rust-anything app replay . # the original must pass 100% rust-anything app replay . --build "target/release/mytool" ``` - `app record` runs the original on the app's own documented examples (`$ mytool ...` lines in its Markdown and shell files, with the files they name), an `--inputs` JSONL file (`{"name", "args", "stdin", "env", "files"}`), and semantic traps derived from those cases (non-ASCII and emoji strings, negative division and modulo, overflow, large and tiny floats, map order, missing files). Each case runs twice; what differs between the two runs becomes a `[..]` wildcard. `--normalize timestamps|uuids|key-order` or `--normalize name=regex` adds normalizers, saved with the cases. - Cases are [trycmd](https://docs.rs/trycmd) files in `rust/app-cases/`: `.toml` (argv, env, exit code), `.stdin`, `.stdout`, `.stderr`, `.in/` (files in) and `.out/` (files written). Read and edit them by hand; a Rust test can run them with `trycmd` once the port has a binary. - `app replay` runs any build against the cases, prints `passed/total`, writes `rust/app-cases/replay-report.md` with a diff per failing case, and exits non-zero on any mismatch. A build that appends to the file named by `RUST_ANYTHING_FALLBACK_LOG` (one line per fallback to the original), as the front door below does, also gets its fallback rate reported. - `app replay --case ` reruns one case by the name the report gives it: the fast, repeatable loop for fixing a mismatch before running everything again. Then move the entry point to Rust and hand it commands one unit at a time: ```sh rust-anything app front-door . # rust/app: every command runs the original rust-anything app wire . textkit --command upper # after textkit-rs passes gate # write the glue in rust/app/src/units/textkit.rs, then: rust-anything app wire . textkit # 100% again, lower fallback rate ``` - `app front-door` scaffolds `rust/app`, a Rust binary named after the app: a clap parser for the commands and flags in the recorded cases, where every command runs the original with the same argv, stdin and environment and passes its output and exit code through. Each fallback is counted, so replaying the fresh front door gives 100% passed at 100% fallback (it builds and replays to show it). It never overwrites `rust/app`: the code is yours from then on. - `app wire --command ` runs `gate` on the unit crate (`--skip-gate` if it just passed), adds it to `rust/app` as a library, writes `src/units/.rs` once for you or your agent to fill in (parse the arguments, call `::port`, print what the original prints), routes the commands to it, then builds and replays. `RUST_ANYTHING_UNIT_=original` sends a wired unit back to the original until the lift. Wire the app's own name as a command (`--command mytool`) for argv that names no command: no arguments, unknown commands, usage errors. When replay passes with fallback rate 0 and every unit passes gate, make it a pure Rust app: ```sh rust-anything app lift . ``` - `app lift` refuses until both hold, and says what blocks it: the cases still falling back, glue still a stub, units failing gate. - On a copy first, it removes the fallback path and the kill switches, turns each unit crate into a plain library of `rust/app` (no `cdylib`, bindings or generated wrappers), and adds `rust/app/tests/app_cases.rs`, which runs `rust/app-cases` with trycmd on `cargo test`, so CI needs nothing but cargo. - Then it runs the lift checklist: fmt, clippy `-D warnings` and tests on every unit and on `rust/app`, every target named in `rust/DECISIONS.md` built or checked where it is installed, files read at run time and asset folders not embedded, and replay on the pure binary. Only when all of it passes are the changes written back. The original is never touched. ### Servers The same commands prove HTTP servers. `--http` says the command starts a server; it takes its port from `PORT` or `{port}` in the command (`--port` for one that always listens on the same port): ```sh rust-anything app record . --http -- node server.js rust-anything app replay . rust-anything app front-door . # axum: every route proxied rust-anything app wire . api --route 'GET /users/{id}' --route '*' rust-anything app lift . ``` - Requests come from `curl` lines in the app's docs (`curl -X POST -d ... http://localhost:8080/x`), `--inputs` (`{"name", "method", "path", "headers", "body"}`) and traps: path segments and query values swapped for the same traps as CLI arguments, bodies for text and JSON traps, and an unknown route. Each run starts the server fresh and sends the requests in name order, so state between requests is kept. - Cases are `rust/app-cases/http/.toml` (the request, the status and the headers that matter) and `.body` (the response body, with `[..]` where two runs differed). Date, server and other per-response headers are left out; delete any header line you do not care about. - The front door is an axum server that starts the original on a port of its own and proxies every route no unit answers. `wire --route` takes axum routes: `METHOD /path/{param}`, `/path` for any method, `*` for everything else; the glue gets the route, its parameters and the request. `lift` removes the proxy; HTTP cases then run in CI with `app replay`. ### Libraries A library has no process to replay: its public API is the front door, and each unit's recorded cases are the proof. ```sh rust-anything app front-door . # rust/app: a Rust crate with the public API # each unit through the loop: bridge, record, port.rs, build, diff, gate; then: rust-anything app wire . textkit-rs # re-exported from rust/app; the original imports its shadow rust-anything app replay . # every wired unit's cases; fallback = exports still in the original rust-anything app lift . ``` - `app front-door` finds the public API (every unit's exports) when the repository has no `main` and no server (`--library` otherwise), and scaffolds `rust/app` as a library crate. Each wired unit becomes a module of it: `pub use textkit_rs::port as textkit;`. - `app wire` takes a crate made by `bridge`, runs `gate`, and writes the unit's shadow drop-in: the original package imports it in place of the unit, so its callers keep the original API and reach the Rust. `RUST_ANYTHING_UNIT_=original` sends the unit back (C: build without the shadow's flags). - `app replay` runs every wired unit's recorded cases through its bindings. The fallback rate is the share of public exports Rust does not answer yet: unwired units, and exports `bridge` keeps in the original language. - `app lift` needs fallback 0 and every unit through `gate`; it strips the bindings, wrappers and shadows from the units and leaves `rust/app` as one pure Rust library. It does not touch any `port.rs`, so the cases that matched through the bindings still describe it; the checklist warns about files of the original that still import the shadows. All five are MCP tools too: `app_record`, `app_replay`, `app_front_door`, `app_wire` and `app_lift`. ## Case study: x18n's core All 29 functions of x18n's core that can move without an API change were ported with rust-anything: every gate passes and 7,925 recorded cases match exactly. `rust-anything bench` then showed the ports are slower than the TS as called from JS, because the bridge costs more than the work. Full report: [`demo/x18n-core`](./demo/x18n-core/README.md). The lesson is built in: measure with `bench` before shipping a port. ## Hot paths: keep the data in Rust A port called once per item pays the bridge once per item, and loses to a JIT. What wins is moving the loop: `profile` finds it, and `--batch` generates a class that takes the items once and runs the function over all of them per call, on all cores, with typed-array results. ```sh rust-anything profile ../x18n -- node --experimental-strip-types $PWD/demo/x18n-search/search.ts . # -> fuzzyScore: a quarter of the run, called per key by `matched`: batch it rust-anything bridge ../x18n packages/core/src/fuzzy.ts --batch fuzzyScore:text ``` ```js const search = new FuzzyScoreBatch(keys) // once const order = search.rank(query, 0) // per keystroke: indexes, best first ``` A `FuzzyScoreIndex` struct in `port.rs` replaces the default loop with one that prepares the items once, and can rank by itself (`rank`): it keeps the keys lowercased with a character mask each, a table of each key's first position of every common character (a one-letter query is one column), and the last query's matches (typing `se` after `s` rescores only what `s` matched). On x18n's sidebar search over 50,000 keys, typed letter by letter, with identical results: | | Per query | vs TS | | --- | ---: | ---: | | TS: `map(fuzzyScore)`, filter, sort | 10 ms | 1x | | TS with the same narrowing as the index | 4.1-5.4 ms | 2x | | The same port, called per key | - | 0.2-0.4x | | `FuzzyScoreBatch`, default index (4 cores) | 5.1 ms | 1.7x | | `FuzzyScoreBatch` with `FuzzyScoreIndex` (napi, 4 cores) | 0.45-0.56 ms | **18-22x** | | The same with wasm (one thread) | 0.95 ms | **11.5x** | Against TS doing the same narrowing, Rust is still 7-12x faster (wasm 5x). Turn the returned indexes into keys with a plain loop: `Array.from(order, i => keys[i])` cost 20x more, 0.4 ms. Every language gets batches, and they beat the original even where per-call ports lose. The same work on 4 cores, identical results and errors (benchmarks in each demo folder): | Language | Workload | Original | Per-call port vs original | Batch vs original | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | TS | x18n search, 50,000 keys | 10 ms | 0.2-0.4x | **20x** | | Python | `slugify`, 20,000 strings | 98 ms | - | **17x** | | Ruby | `slugify`, 20,000 strings | 110 ms | - | **12.7x** | | Ruby | `shellescape` (stdlib), 50,000 mixed values | 88 ms | - | **11.8x** | | Go | `Slugify`, 50,000 strings | 49 ms | 0.93x | **4x** | | Java | `slugify`, 50,000 strings | 43 ms | 0.68x | **3x** | Compiled originals gain less: the per-item work is already fast, so the batch wins by the number of cores. Batch crates allocate with mimalloc: with the system allocator the Go batch was slower than one thread. Demo: [`demo/x18n-search`](./demo/x18n-search/README.md). ## Real code in six languages Go's `path`, Ruby's `shellwords`, Python's `colorsys`, JDK and glibc behavior behind small facades: every port passes its gate, 13,010 recorded cases in all. The runs found and fixed bugs in rust-anything (floats off by one ULP through `serde_json`, C crashes during recording, untyped code getting garbage inputs). Called per function, the Ruby port runs 4.4x faster than Ruby and the Python port 1.35x faster than CPython, while Go and Java leaf functions stay faster in their own language; as batches, all of them win (see the table above). Report: [`docs/real-world-languages.md`](./docs/real-world-languages.md). ## Example: a real module from x18n `packages/core/src/fuzzy.ts` from [x18n](https://github.com/x18n-dev/x18n), ported both ways in [`demo/`](./demo): ```sh rust-anything analyze ../x18n # fuzzy.ts: ready, wasm-bindgen (core runs in browsers) rust-anything bridge ../x18n packages/core/src/fuzzy.ts --out demo/fuzzy-rs rust-anything record demo/fuzzy-rs --count 2000 # write src/port.rs rust-anything gate demo/fuzzy-rs ``` A first port that indexed by Rust `char` passed simple tests but failed `diff`: ``` 198/200 cases match - fuzzyScore("b😀", "a😀b😀c"): expected {"ok":1997}, got {"ok":1998} ``` JS `indexOf` counts UTF-16 code units, so an emoji is two positions. The port in `demo/*/src/port.rs` uses the generated `utf16` helpers and passes 2000/2000 cases and the gate, as napi-rs (`demo/fuzzy-napi`) and as wasm-bindgen (`demo/fuzzy-rs`). The plan rust-anything writes for all of x18n: [`docs/examples/x18n.md`](./docs/examples/x18n.md). ## Install ```sh cargo install --path . ``` `record`, `diff` and `bench` run the original in its own runtime: Node 22.6+ for TS (it runs `.ts` sources directly), Python 3.9+ for Python and C (ctypes), Go 1.21+, Ruby 3+, JDK 17+ (`javac` and `java`). C also needs a C compiler. wasm bridges also need `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli --version --locked`; `build` names the exact version. For agents, `rust-anything setup` registers everything (see Quick start). To add the MCP server to one project by hand instead (`.mcp.json`): ```json { "mcpServers": { "rust-anything": { "command": "rust-anything", "args": ["mcp"] } } } ``` ## What `bridge` decides - Exports that cannot cross a bridge stay in the source language, with the reason, and the shadow module re-exports the original. For TS: functions that take or return functions, generators and iterators, RegExp, `instanceof` checks, generics, and values whose types (followed through imports, re-exports and `extends`) hold functions. `--keep "name: reason"` keeps more, e.g. code that depends on `Intl` data. - TS types map to Rust types, with type aliases resolved through imports and parameter types inferred from default values; structured values cross as a generated binary wire (JSON only as a fallback for shapes the wire does not model). - JSON cannot express `undefined`, NaN, Infinity, -0 or lone surrogates: structured values carry markers (`{"$undefined": true}`, `{"$num": "NaN"}`, `{"$utf16": [...]}`) that the generated `index.cjs` translates, with helpers in the crate's `js.rs`. `record` runs TS sources as they are: a Node resolve hook follows bundler-style imports (`./errors` to `./errors.ts`), `--resolve-from` supplies npm packages when the repo has none installed, and TS that needs transforming (enums, parameter properties) is retried with `--experimental-transform-types`. ## What `analyze` looks at - Packages (`package.json`) and source files; skips `node_modules`, build output, fixtures, playgrounds, tool configs. ﻿# mcp-for-blender-pro

### Your Blender scene. Your AI models. One creative workspace.


**An AI assistant for Blender that can inspect your scene, build objects, edit materials, find assets and carry out multi-step workflows—with a visual chat workspace and a built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.**


![Blender 4.2+](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blender-4.2%2B-E87D0D?logo=blender&logoColor=white)
![Release 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/release-1.0.0-98D85B)
![Windows x64](https://img.shields.io/badge/download-Windows_x64-357EC7)
![MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue)


[Download](https://github.com/bookwjitchieni1986/blender-ai-mcp-addon/releases/latest) · [Getting started](docs/QUICKSTART.md) · [Connections and agents](docs/CONNECTIONS.md)


![AI chat workspace with a live Blender scene preview](docs/images/studio.png)


## Turn a creative brief into scene operations


Start with an idea. Ask the assistant to inspect your scene, create a product-display layout, arrange objects, assign materials or prepare an export. Follow its actions in the conversation and inspect the result in the viewport preview. Keep working in Blender throughout the process.


**mcp-for-blender-pro brings conversation, scene tools, model choice and agent workflows together.** It is designed for artists who want faster iteration, technical artists who automate repetitive work, and developers connecting AI tools to Blender.


## Why choose mcp-for-blender-pro?


| Capability | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| **Blender-aware assistance** | Scene and object inspection gives the assistant context before it acts. |
| **A visual Studio workspace** | Chat, scene objects, viewport snapshots, approvals and a task board in a companion window. |
| **Your choice of AI** | Connect supported cloud providers, local Ollama models or compatible custom endpoints. |
| **Saved connections** | Keep work and personal connections separate, including multiple keys for the same provider. |
| **One assistant or a team** | Use a single model for quick changes, or managers, workers and reviewers for structured tasks. |
| **Built-in MCP server** | Connect OpenCode and other clients supporting authenticated Streamable HTTP MCP. |
| **21 scene tools** | Create, inspect, edit, capture, search assets, consult Blender APIs and export scenes. |
| **Multilingual menus** | Choose English, German, French, Spanish or Chinese for the main interface. |


## From a quick edit to an agent team


Use **Single assistant** for direct, conversational work. For larger tasks, configure a **Team chain** with individual responsibilities, instructions and models.


- **Manager:** breaks the request into assignments and acceptance criteria.
- **Workers:** perform the assigned scene operations.
- **Reviewers:** inspect results and approve work or return specific findings.


Tasks run sequentially so scene edits stay ordered. A blocked task gets one correction attempt; a second failed review stops the workflow. The task board exposes assignments, attempts and review findings as work progresses.


![Agent roles and model configuration](docs/images/studio-team.png)


## Connect the models that fit your work


Supported connections include **OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, OpenCode Zen, Ollama and custom APIs**. Load the available model catalog and select a model directly in Blender or Studio.


Custom endpoints support OpenAI Chat Completions, Anthropic Messages and Ollama protocols. Choose models with tool-calling support; image-capable models can also interpret viewport screenshots. OpenCode-only free models are available through the OpenCode client.


![Provider, saved connection and model selection](docs/images/studio-settings.png)


## Install and create


1. Download **`mcp-for-blender-pro.zip`** from [Releases](../../releases/latest).
2. In Blender, open **Edit → Preferences → Get Extensions → menu → Install from Disk**.
3. Select the ZIP, enable **mcp-for-blender-pro**, then open **3D Viewport → N → MCP Pro**.
4. Choose a provider, add your connection details and select a model.
5. Send a message in Blender or click **Open Studio Window**.


The release bundle targets **Windows x64 with Blender 4.2 or later**. Keep Blender open while using Studio or an external client.


### Try these prompts


> Inspect this scene and explain its object structure before making any changes.


> Create a simple product-display scene with a pedestal, a camera and three lights. Give the pedestal a matte blue material.


> Duplicate the selected object into a neatly spaced row of five and show the viewport.


> Find an appropriate Poly Haven asset for this scene and ask before importing it.


## Blender automation through MCP


Launch **OpenCode Portable** from the sidebar to work through OpenCode with the Blender connection configured for you. OpenCode manages its own provider sign-in and model selection. Other compatible MCP clients can connect to the authenticated local endpoint described in the [connection guide](docs/CONNECTIONS.md).


| Tool group | Included tools |
|---|---|
| Scene inspection | `get_scene_info`, `list_objects`, `get_object_info` |
| Object creation | `add_cube`, `add_sphere`, `add_cylinder`, `add_plane`, `add_light`, `add_camera` |
| Editing | `move_object`, `duplicate_object`, `delete_object`, `parent_objects`, `set_material` |
| Visual feedback and scripting | `viewport_screenshot`, `execute_code` |
| Blender API and export | `bpy_api_lookup`, `describe_node_type`, `export_scene` |
| Asset workflows | `search_assets`, `import_asset` |


Asset integrations include **Poly Haven, Sketchfab and Poly Pizza**. Configure service keys where required and follow the licenses of the assets you use.


## Stay in control of your scene


Built-in chat supports operation approvals, cancellation after the current step and named undo steps for mutations. Python tool validation helps catch disallowed operations; it is not a security sandbox. External MCP clients manage their own approval policies.


Connection credentials are stored in your user settings. Chat history lasts for the current session. Studio runs locally and authenticates requests to Blender.


## Keywords

# NeonClipping

**Paste a link. Get captioned 9:16 clips in about two minutes. Free, local, open-source.**

NeonClipping turns long YouTube / Twitch / Kick videos (or your own MP4) into vertical, captioned clips with a title and hook for each. Everything runs on your machine: no account, no subscription, no upload.

[![Star on GitHub](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/iamajmeena/neonclipping?style=for-the-badge&logo=github&label=Star%20on%20GitHub)](https://github.com/iamajmeena/neonclipping) [![Instagram](https://img.shields.io/badge/Follow-%40iamajmeena-E4405F?style=for-the-badge&logo=instagram&logoColor=white)](https://www.instagram.com/iamajmeena/)

🌐 **Website with one-click Windows setup:** <https://iamajmeena.github.io/neonclipping/>

**Made by [Ajay K Meena](https://www.instagram.com/iamajmeena/)** (Director, DOP, colorist, DaVinci Resolve educator, Jaipur). If NeonClipping saves you time, please ⭐ star the repo and follow [@iamajmeena](https://www.instagram.com/iamajmeena/) on Instagram.

![demo](docs/demo.gif)

![UI](docs/neonclipping-ui.jpg)

📘 **Guides (Hindi + English, PDF):** [docs/NeonClipping-Guide-EN-HI.pdf](docs/NeonClipping-Guide-EN-HI.pdf)  
🤖 **Let an AI agent install it for you:** copy [docs/NEONCLIPPING-AGENT-SETUP-PROMPT.txt](docs/NEONCLIPPING-AGENT-SETUP-PROMPT.txt) into Claude Code, Codex CLI or Cursor.

## How it finds good moments

Two modes, one button.

**⚡ Fast mode (default, videos over 10 min)** copies the trick that makes the fastest clippers fast: never look at the whole video.

1. Download **audio only** (79 MB for an 85-minute video, about 10 s).
2. Take the transcript for free from YouTube's own captions (word-timed). No speech model needed. For other sources a local Whisper model is used as the fallback.
3. Score the whole audio track for *sudden loudness jumps* (vs a 2-minute local baseline), *raised voices* (2–4 kHz energy) and quiet-to-loud transitions.
4. Take the best moments, read each one's transcript with a local LLM (Ollama) and let it score the moment, write a title and a hook. Snap the start and end to sentence boundaries inside your Min/Max length.
5. Download **only the chosen sections** of the video (not the whole file), trim exactly by matching their sound to the audio track, and render 1080x1920 clips with burned-in captions.

**🔬 Deep mode** downloads the whole video, adds optical-flow motion (OpenCV Farneback: fast objects, impacts, camera whips) and cut density to the audio signals, shortlists 4× more candidates and gives the LLM 15 seconds of context before and after each one.

Measured on one machine (RTX 2060, 16 threads), Fast mode, 3 clips each:

| Source | Time |
|---|---|
| 85-minute YouTube stream (YouTube captions) | **97 s** |
| 3-hour Twitch VOD (no captions, local speech model) | **136 s** |
| 90-second YouTube trailer | 21 s |
| 90-second local MP4 | 14 s |

Your numbers depend on network and CPU.

## How it decides what is a good moment

Every candidate moment is scored from several signals, then the best ones are kept:

| Signal | What it looks for |
|---|---|
| Loudness jump | A sudden boom or shout compared with the last two minutes |
| Raised voice | Energy in the 2–4 kHz band (screaming, yelling) |
| What is said | "oh my god", "oh shit", "run", "police", "bhaago", "arre yaar" and similar (English, Hinglish, Hindi) |
| On-screen action | Fast motion (optical flow), explosion-like flashes, red/blue light flicker, scene cuts |
| AI score | A small local LLM reads the transcript: emotion, punchline, payoff |

**It learns from you.** Under every clip there are 5 stars. Your ratings stay on your computer (`data/feedback.jsonl`). After 8 ratings the weights of the signals above are re-fitted (ridge regression pulled toward the defaults, blended in gradually), so a gamer-shouting-heavy taste ranks shouting higher and a calm-explainer taste ranks it lower. Nothing is uploaded.

## Features

- One-click **Make clips**, live progress, clips appear one by one with preview and MP4 download.
- **Min / Max clip length** (e.g. 30–80 s). Clips end on a sentence.
- **Facecam position presets** (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right, bottom-centre, none) for the usual streamer layouts, remembered between sessions. Or draw the face and gameplay boxes yourself in the editor.
- **11 native layouts:** camera above/below gameplay, blurred fill, full-screen crop, gameplay only, four corner overlays, circle facecam and side-by-side. Independent face/game selection and a face-size slider. Preview-only platform safe zones.
- Caption styles: GTA Neon, Impact, Clean, Hormozi and MrBeast. Word-timed, editable words, SRT export.
- **Hinglish captions**: Hindi speech is written in English letters ("kya haal hai bhai") by default. Pick Hinglish / हिंदी / English explicitly if you like. Caption accuracy: Fast, Accurate (Whisper large-v3-turbo, default) or Best Hindi (large-v3, much slower on small GPUs).
- **Make clips uses your own setup**: facecam preset or the boxes you draw in step 03.
- Optical-flow motion + audio highlight ranking, frame-accurate NVENC export (falls back to x264).
- Nothing leaves your computer. The server binds to `127.0.0.1` only.

## Change clips after generating them

![Saved clip editor with eleven layouts](docs/saved-clip-editor.jpg)

Open **My clips → Edit clip**. The saved editor includes all **11 speaker position/shape layouts**, a speaker-size slider, editable subtitle words, caption style and caption height.

- **Apply to this clip** updates the opened clip.
- **Apply to this video's clips** updates the currently saved clips associated with the same source URL. Each keeps its own timestamps, transcript, title and hook. New clips still being generated are not included in that snapshot.
- Source download, highlight discovery and speech recognition are **not repeated**. Burned-in captions and framing require encoding a new final MP4.
- Original source files must remain in `data/`. Previous MP4s are kept; the library displays the latest versions. Old exports missing saved word timings can recover captions from their SRT, with approximate per-word timing.
- This edits the selected moments; changing the clip's start/end or spoken language requires a separate trim/transcription workflow.

Validation on one 796.9-second source: all 11 layouts and five caption styles exported with audio and decoded successfully. A seven-clip layout/style update took 119.58 seconds while reusing each clip's exact source, range and word list. These are local checks, not guaranteed runtimes or a caption-quality benchmark.

Run the portable regression tests with `python -m unittest discover -s tests -v`.

## Install

**Easiest (Windows):** download [`NeonClipping-Setup.bat`](https://github.com/iamajmeena/neonclipping/releases/latest/download/NeonClipping-Setup.bat) from the [website](https://iamajmeena.github.io/neonclipping/) or the Releases page and double-click it. It checks your PC, installs Python and FFmpeg if missing, installs NeonClipping into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\NeonClipping`, creates a Desktop shortcut and opens the app. Mac/Linux: `install.sh` (new, not yet tested on a real Mac). Or follow the steps below.

Requirements: Python 3.10+, FFmpeg on PATH. Optional but recommended: [Ollama](https://ollama.com) with `ollama pull llama3.2:3b` for AI titles, hooks and scores (without it clips are picked by the audio/motion score), and an NVIDIA GPU for NVENC and faster-whisper.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/iamajmeena/neonclipping
cd neonclipping
# Windows
./run.ps1
# Linux / macOS
./run.sh
```

Open <http://127.0.0.1:8770>, paste a link, press **⚡ Make clips**.

Optional GPU speech model support (only used when a video has no YouTube captions):

```bash
.venv/bin/pip install nvidia-cublas-cu12 "nvidia-cudnn-cu12==9.*"
```

Set `NEONCLIPPING_CPU=1` to force CPU. Set `NEONCLIPPING_PORT=9000` to use another port.

## How it is built

| File | Job |
|---|---|
| `app.py` | FastAPI server, `/make` pipeline, export, library |
| `smart.py` | Moment scoring: transcript + local LLM, sentence snapping |
| `highlights.py` | Audio-jump / shout / optical-flow / cut ranking, parallel decode |
| `captions_yt.py` | YouTube word-timed captions (json3) parser |
| `captions.py` | Local Whisper (GPU first, CPU fallback), ASS/SRT styles |
| `translit.py` | Devanagari → Hinglish (word by word, keeps timings) |
| `standalone.py`, `previews.py` | Link import, early preview frames |

## Live clipping (while the stream is on)

Paste a Twitch channel link or a YouTube Live link into the **Live clipping** panel and press Start. NeonClipping records the stream (Streamlink), reads chat anonymously, counts messages in 10 s buckets and cuts a clip around every chat spike (chat velocity more than 2.5 sigma and 2.5x the 5-minute baseline). The clip starts about 24 s *before* the spike, because chat reacts after the moment. It then gets captions, a hook and title, your layout and facecam boxes, and a viral score like any other clip. **Clip the last 30 s now** cuts on demand, **Stop** ends the session. It only works while the stream is live; for finished videos use Make clips.

There is also a command-line version in `live/live_clip.py`.

## Creators (clip a streamer automatically)

Add a Twitch name or a Twitch / YouTube channel link in the **Creators** panel. NeonClipping checks every minute; when that creator goes live it records the stream and clips the chat spikes, using the layout, facecam boxes and caption style you had selected when you added them (“Use my current layout” updates it). Clips appear under the creator and in My clips.

- One stream at a time (recording and rendering are heavy); other creators wait their turn.
- NeonClipping must stay open. Unattended recordings stop after 3 hours (a new one starts if the creator is still live), stop when less than 8 GB of disk is free, and the big recording file is deleted after the last clip is cut.
- Pressing **Stop** pauses that creator for 30 minutes; switching Auto off and on resumes at once.
- Tested on Twitch (recording, chat spikes, clip, feed). YouTube channels are detected through yt-dlp; an auto-clipped YouTube stream was not run end to end.

## Tests

`tests/` holds an end-to-end suite that runs against the live server: page and API validation, every layout and caption style rendered and measured, editing one / all clips of a video, Make clips on real YouTube / Twitch / local sources in every mode and language, live clipping on a real stream, the creator list, star ratings, the installer and the website. Unit tests cover the chat-spike rule, caption grouping and re-editing. The last full run is in [`tests/REPORT.md`](tests/REPORT.md): 187 checks, all passing, plus the 12 problems the run found and fixed.

```
python -m unittest tests.test_captions tests.test_live tests.test_reedit
python tests/e2e.py static export edit creators feedback   # server must be running
python tests/e2e_make.py          # real downloads + transcription (about 25 min)
python tests/e2e_live.py          # needs a Twitch channel that is live
python tests/e2e_site.py          # website, links, release assets
python tests/make_report.py       # rebuild tests/REPORT.md
```

## Style & extras

- **Templates:** wrap the clip in an *X post* (light or dark), a *TikTok hook* box or a *Breaking news* broadcast frame. Type the name, handle and hook; the card, avatar letter, check mark and ticker are drawn for you.
- **Background card:** padded, rounded-corner video card on a blurred copy, a colour, a gradient or your own image (dimmed, blurred).
- **Logo / watermark** (4 corners, size, opacity), **credit line** (or "Clip: channel name" automatically), **outro ribbon** that slides in for the last seconds.
- **Music bed:** one track under the voice that rises to a peak volume in the last seconds (volume, peak and riser length are yours).
- **Six caption animations:** highlight (word by word), pop-in, pop-in line, one by one, build up, full line.
- **Import captions:** drop an `.srt` or `.ass` file; the words are timed to the clip and can be edited.
- All of it works in Make clips, single exports and "Edit saved clips" (including "apply to all clips of this video").

## Find my facecam

The **Find my facecam** chip (or "find it automatically when I press Make clips") looks at 14 frames of the video, finds rectangles whose border stays in the same place, and keeps the one that holds a face (small local YuNet face model, MIT licence, `models/`). It rejects the game's minimap and HUD panels, finds webcams in a corner or floating on a side, and answers "no facecam" when it is not sure. Measured on 30 real saved streams: found the webcam on every stream that has one; clean "not found" on trailers and talking-head videos. Not perfect: some boxes cover only the face inside a framed webcam.

## Long streams with a free chatbot

**AI parts** (below step 01): paste a YouTube link, NeonClipping splits the video's captions into ~25-minute parts and gives a copy-ready prompt per part. Paste each into any free chatbot, paste all answers back (JSON or lines like `12:30-13:10 title`), tick the moments and press Make clips: only those sections are downloaded and rendered. A chatbot given a 9-hour transcript in one go only reads the start; small parts fix that. Nothing is sent anywhere by NeonClipping; the chatbot step is manual.

## Honest limits

- Highlight picking is a heuristic plus a small local LLM. It finds loud, energetic, quotable moments, not guaranteed "viral" ones. Review before posting.
- The action cues (motion, flash, light flicker) are simple heuristics on a tiny low-resolution copy; they rank moments, they do not recognise "a police chase". Star ratings are how it gets better at your taste.
- The LLM sees text only. It cannot see the screen.
- Without YouTube captions (Twitch VODs, uploaded files) a speech model must transcribe each candidate, which is slow on CPU.
- Auto-caption accuracy follows the source: YouTube's auto captions are imperfect, especially Hinglish.
- Deep mode was verified on a short video only; on multi-hour videos it downloads the whole file first and is slow by design.
- Facecam presets are starting points, not detection: if you pick Bottom-right but the cam is bottom-left, the top half of the clip will show the wrong area. Pick the right corner or draw your own boxes.

## Support

NeonClipping is free. If it saves you time you can ⭐ star the repo, follow [@iamajmeena](https://www.instagram.com/iamajmeena/), or optionally donate via Razorpay (UPI / cards): <https://rzp.io/rzp/JN41CpW>. The app also has a ♥ Donate button. Nothing is ever locked behind a donation.

## Credits and inspiration

Design ideas studied from open-source clippers: [PeakCut](https://github.com/haziqahmedqasmi/PeakCut) (audio-first download, captions as transcript, section download), [ClipCutter](https://github.com/curtyo18/ClipCutter), [content-ai](https://github.com/buddah0/content-ai), and the Growlance live-clipper script. Also studied: PeakCut's facecam-by-static-border idea and creator list (reimplemented here with our own code, plus a face check), the public feature list of the YIZERGE desktop editor (templates, background card, music riser, caption animations; only its public web page was read), and a creator's walkthrough of splitting a 9-hour stream into small transcript parts for a free chatbot. Built on FFmpeg, yt-dlp, FastAPI, faster-whisper, OpenCV (YuNet face detector, MIT), Ollama.

items.name: inference-optimisation-skill
items.description: Agent skill for hill-climbing local LLM serving speed (decode, speculative decoding, prefill, KV, startup, TTFT) on any hardware and quantization
items.readme:
# inference-optimisation An agent skill for **hill-climbing the speed of a local LLM server** on any hardware and any quantization. It covers: - single-user and concurrent decode - speculative decoding - prefill - KV cache size - startup time and time to first token It works under a memory cap, and every result has to survive a full-context stability check. It encodes how we actually got these speedups. It is not a list of flags. The workflow: 1. Compute the theoretical ceiling. 2. Change one thing at a time. 3. Measure against interleaved controls. 4. Log every result, including the failures. 5. Gate on long-context retrieval. 6. Qualify a clean, pinned build before publishing. It works with Claude Code and any agent that loads `SKILL.md`-style skills. Any model can also follow it from [`PROMPT.md`](PROMPT.md). ## What we've been able to accomplish Results from the hill-climbs this skill was distilled from. Every number was measured on the hardware named; see the linked sources for methods and raw data. | Hardware | Model / quant / engine | Before → after | |---|---|---| | **Intel Arc B390 iGPU** (laptop, 64 GB unified LPDDR5X, ~115 GB/s) | Ornith-1.5-35B-A3B, EXL3 4 bpw, SGLang XPU + MTP | Decode, 1 user: 43.6 → **53 tok/s** (median)
Decode, 4 users: 84.7 → **103 tok/s**
Prefill 32K: 1,037 → **1,660 tok/s**
Prefill 256K: 297 → **628 tok/s** (2.1×)
KV cache: 264K tokens → **4 × 256K**
Startup: 113 → **43 s**
Registry Lab gates: decode 28.6 → **41.0**, prefill 255 → **667** | | **Intel Arc Pro B70** | Qwen3.8-27B, EXL3 4 bpw, vLLM + custom XPU kernels | Decode: **91.2 tok/s** at 1 user, **365** at 16 (prose, thinking on)
Same card with llama.cpp Q4_K_M: 25.0
Prefill 4K/32K/128K/254K: 1,654/1,434/928/650 → **2,421/2,259/1,415/911**
Agent-session replay: 193 → **147 s** | | **Intel Arc Pro B70** | Same model, SGLang + the same kernels | Decode, 1 user: **82.6 tok/s**, vs vLLM 75.7 on the same card and day | | **RTX 3090** | Qwen3.8-27B EXL3 3 bpw + MTP | **96.2 tok/s** prose / **141.1** code, 1 user | | **RTX 3090** | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B EXL3 3 bpw + MTP | **251.7 / 357.9 tok/s**, 1 user | | **RTX 3090** | Flash-Next EXL3, 256K context | MTP: 45.5 → **65.6 tok/s** | | **4× H200 NVL** | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, vLLM + speculative decoding | Crashed under load → **229.1 tok/s** decode, **17,546 tok/s** prefill; all six gates pass | Sources: - [local-ai-registry](https://github.com/sybil-solutions/local-ai-registry): - [Ornith B390 recipe](https://github.com/sybil-solutions/local-ai-registry/tree/main/data/sources/ornith-b390-exl3), with the full hill-climb log in [PR #453](https://github.com/sybil-solutions/local-ai-registry/pull/453) - the RTX 3090 and H200 recipes - [trellis-serve](https://github.com/sybil-solutions/trellis-serve): - `xpu/README.md`, `xpu/docs/PROGRESS.md` and `xpu/docs/SGLANG.md` for B70 - `cuda/README.md` for the RTX 3090 - [qwen-serve](https://github.com/sybil-solutions/qwen-serve) ### Reading the B390 result That run is the one this skill grew out of. Its ceiling calculation said: - **Decode:** 100 tok/s for one user was only reachable with two useful speculative drafts. This model's draft head accepts ~14% at depth 2, so the practical target was ~88–97 tok/s. We reached ~55% of it; the rest is GEMV kernel efficiency. - **Prefill at 256K:** we reached 628 tok/s against a ~670–684 tok/s ceiling. The skill makes the agent compute this up front, so it can tell you early when a target is above the physics. ## How it works ``` ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ measure HW ─▶ │ THEORY.md: bytes/token ÷ bandwidth, FLOPs/token ÷ 50% peak, KV │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ baseline ─▶ profile ─▶ pick lever (ceiling gap × likelihood) ─▶ configs/NEW.json ▲ │ │ queue.sh ctl NEW ctl (serialized, AC-only, │ memory watchdog, ≥6 samples, medians) │ │ PLAN.md + ledger.jsonl ◀── accept only if it beats BOTH neighbouring controls ──┘ │ and regresses nothing by >3% ▼ long-context needle gate ─▶ concurrent full-KV soak ─▶ plateau? ─▶ pinned clean build ─▶ acceptance gates ─▶ publish ``` The skill has three parts: **[`SKILL.md`](skills/inference-optimisation/SKILL.md): the procedure.** - Inventory, ceilings, ground rules, the loop and lever order. - When to stop, how to qualify and publish, and how to report. **[`references/`](skills/inference-optimisation/references): loaded only when needed.** - [`ceilings.md`](skills/inference-optimisation/references/ceilings.md): how to compute decode, prefill, TTFT, startup and KV maxima, with a worked example. - [`methodology.md`](skills/inference-optimisation/references/methodology.md): measurement traps. Chunk-counted tokens, mis-sized prompts, acceptance counters, drift, unified-memory accounting. - [`levers.md`](skills/inference-optimisation/references/levers.md): every lever with measured evidence. It is tagged general vs stack-specific. - [`gotchas.md`](skills/inference-optimisation/references/gotchas.md): known traps in vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp and ExLlama, and on Intel, NVIDIA, Apple and AMD hardware. - [`publishing.md`](skills/inference-optimisation/references/publishing.md): pinning, clean builds, the six acceptance gates, proving the build matches the best, results cards. **[`scripts/`](skills/inference-optimisation/scripts): a small, engine-agnostic harness.** It is standard-library Python plus bash. - `bench.py` benchmarks any OpenAI-compatible server. It measures: - startup and short-prompt TTFT; - c1 decode (median of N) and cN aggregate decode; - cold prefill at several lengths; - long-context needle retrieval; - peak memory, with a cap watchdog. It flags looping output, failed requests and runs on battery. Token counts come from server usage stats, never from streamed chunks, and everything lands in `ledger.jsonl`. - `ceiling.py` computes the theoretical ceilings from a JSON of measured bandwidth and FLOPs plus component sizes. - `queue.sh` is a serialized, detachable run queue, for interleaving control/candidate/control runs. - `mem.sh` reports a container's real footprint. That includes driver residency on unified-memory GPUs, which cgroups don't see. ## Install Claude Code (user-level): ```bash git clone https://github.com/sybil-solutions/inference-optimisation-skill mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills cp -r inference-optimisation-skill/skills/inference-optimisation ~/.claude/skills/ ``` Then ask, for example: - "hill-climb decode and prefill for the model on :8000 under a 40 GiB cap" - "what's the theoretical max tok/s for this model on this machine?" Other agents: point them at `skills/inference-optimisation/SKILL.md`, or paste [`PROMPT.md`](PROMPT.md) as the task prompt. ## Quick start without an agent ```bash S=skills/inference-optimisation python3 $S/scripts/ceiling.py $S/examples/ceiling-ornith-b390.json # ceilings mkdir -p configs && cp $S/examples/config-existing-server.json configs/base.json # edit base_url/model python3 $S/scripts/bench.py run configs/base.json --long 131072 # one run bash $S/scripts/queue.sh base cand base # interleaved A/B python3 $S/scripts/bench.py show # ledger table ``` ## Principles that carried the most weight - **Ceilings first.** If you don't know the maximum, you can't tell whether 53 tok/s is great or bad, or whether "100 tok/s" is possible. - **Noise is ±5–10%.** Most single-run "wins" are drift. Interleave controls and use medians. - **Measure what matters:** - real tokens, not stream chunks; - real prompt lengths, from the tokenizer; - real memory, including GPU residency on unified memory. - **Speculative decoding is about per-step cost, not acceptance.** - Prune the draft head's vocabulary. - Sweep draft length per concurrency and context. - Keep sampling on the GPU. - **Prove full-context stability** with exact-match needles and a concurrent full-KV soak before calling anything "best". - **Write down failures.** Most of the value in `PLAN.md` is the list of things that did *not* work and why. ## Contributing PRs with new levers, gotchas or results are welcome. Each needs the hardware, model, quantization, engine version, before → after numbers, how they were measured, and a link to raw data. ## License MIT

items.name: fast-anything
items.description: Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow: profile Python, Node or Ruby apps, port the hot functions with your coding agent, prove they behave the same.
items.readme:
Don't rewrite it in Rust. Rewrite the 5% that's slow.

Rewriting a whole app in Rust costs months, minute-long compiles and gigabytes of `target/`. Most of the runtime sits in a few functions anyway. **fast-anything** finds those functions, has your coding agent port *only them* to Rust, proves the port gives the same results on real recorded calls, and swaps it in. One command, fully reversible.

## Install ```sh npm i -g @el4cteo/fast-anything # or: cargo install fast-anything ``` Ports are compiled with your Rust toolchain ([rustup](https://rustup.rs)). ## Use ```sh fast-anything go --agent claude -- python app.py # or: -- node app.ts / bun app.ts / deno run -A app.ts / ruby app.rb / java App.java / mvn exec:java / gradle run / go run . / php app.php / clang -O2 main.c ``` Or step by step: | command | what it does | |---|---| | `scan -- ` | profiles the app, ranks functions by time × how portable they are | | `port [id]` | records up to 500 real calls, creates a one-function Rust crate + `TASK.md` | | `verify` | release-builds the port and replays every recorded call | | `enable` / `disable` | swaps the Rust in or out (one marked block, removed byte for byte) | | `bench` | times the whole app, original vs Rust, interleaved runs | | `report` | markdown + SVG card for your PR | | `doctor` | checks Rust, your runtimes and your agents | `--agent` takes `claude`, `codex`, or any command that reads a prompt on stdin. Without it, hand `TASK.md` to whatever you use. ## Proof, not vibes

That port looked right but compared bytes instead of characters. 148 of 500 real calls caught it. On top of the recorded calls, fast-anything derives extra cases and lets the original answer them: edge cases (NaN, ±infinity, -0.0, zero and ±1, non-ASCII text, empty and up to 16× bigger inputs) and shrunk inputs (tiny and random slices). Nothing is enabled until every case matches: same values (floats within 1e-9), errors where the original errors. A port that is right but slower per call than the original (calling into Rust costs more than the work saved) isn't enabled either. `FAST_ANYTHING_DISABLE=1` runs the original any time. ## Results Real runs on an i5-10500, Windows 11 (C and C++: a 4-core GitHub Actions Linux runner). Reproduce them from [`examples/`](examples). | app | before | after | |---|---|---| | Python fuzzy dedupe (700 names) | 4.91s | **42ms, 116×** | | TypeScript fuzzy dedupe (2,000 names) | 3.11s | **155ms, 20×** | | PHP fuzzy dedupe (600 names) | 2.94s | **53ms, 55×** | | Go fuzzy dedupe (3,000 names) | 3.02s | **144ms, 21×** | | Ruby fuzzy dedupe (400 names) | 3.13s | **228ms, 14×** | | C# fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) | 4.03s | **312ms, 13×** | | Java fuzzy dedupe (4,000 names) | 3.50s | **1.18s, 3×** (11× on the function; the rest is JVM startup) | | C mandelbrot (8 zoom levels) | 431ms | **127ms, 3.4×** | | C++ fuzzy dedupe (6,000 names) | 3.02s | **1.09s, 2.7×** | fast-anything ports the outermost loop it can, not the tiny function called inside it, so the app crosses into Rust once instead of millions of times. Porting only the inner `levenshtein` gave 35× and 1.9×. ## Why not rewrite it all? - **Compile time**: each port is a one-function crate. Seconds, not minutes. - **Cache**: every port shares one `.fast/target`. Delete it whenever you like. - **Risk**: your code stays as it is. Rust is opt-in per function, checked against real behavior. ## Agents - **Claude Code plugin**: `/plugin marketplace add EL4CTEO/fast-anything`, then `/plugin install fast-anything@fast-anything` and `/fast-anything:fast python app.py` - **MCP server** (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor…), built into the binary: `claude mcp add fast-anything -- fast-anything mcp`. 8 tools: `fast_scan`, `fast_port`, `fast_verify`, `fast_enable`, `fast_disable`, `fast_bench`, `fast_report`, `fast_status`. - **Skill**: [`skills/fast-anything`](skills/fast-anything/SKILL.md) teaches any agent the loop. ## Languages | language | binding | status | |---|---|---| | Python 3.10+ | PyO3 | ✅ | | JavaScript / TypeScript (Node 22+, Bun, Deno 2+: `bun app.ts`, `deno run -A app.ts`) | napi-rs | ✅ | | Ruby 3.3+ | C ABI + JSON, through Ruby's built-in Fiddle | ✅ | | Java 22+ (`java App.java`, Maven, Gradle) | the same C bridge, through the FFM API | ✅ | | Kotlin/JVM (Gradle, `src/main/kotlin`, JDK 22+) | the Java bridge; top-level functions, `object` and companion members, extension functions | ✅ | | Go 1.22+ (`go run .`) | the same C bridge, through the Windows loader or dlopen (cgo) | ✅ | | PHP 8.1+ (`php app.php`) | the same C bridge, through PHP's FFI extension (`extension=ffi`) | ✅ | | C and C++ (gcc, clang or Intel oneAPI icx/icpx: `clang -O2 main.c lib.c`) | the same C bridge, through LoadLibrary or dlopen | ✅ | | C# / .NET 8+ (`dotnet run -c Release`) | the same C bridge, through NativeLibrary; profiled with EventPipe, nothing to install | ✅ | It ports top-level, deterministic functions that take plain data (numbers, strings, lists, dicts, typed arrays…), including ones in your entry script when its main code sits under `if __name__ == "__main__":` (or `if __FILE__ == $0`, or `if (import.meta.main)` / `if (require.main === module)`). In Python that means module-level functions and `@staticmethod`s (dataclasses, NamedTuples and numeric NumPy arrays count as plain data), in Java, C# and PHP static methods (and PHP functions), in Go plain functions, in C and C++ free functions and static methods. `scan` says why anything else can't move yet. With Intel oneAPI on Windows, run fast-anything from a shell where `setvars.bat` ran (it sets up the linker). SYCL kernels run on the device and aren't ported; with `-fsycl`, only host functions are profiled and ported. Ruby, Java, Go, PHP, C, C++ and C# need no headers, bindings or extra tools: the port is a plain Rust library with one C entry point taking and returning JSON, and fast-anything replays the recorded calls against it directly. Any language that can call C can use that bridge. ## License MIT
